mcqs.question: What does converting an SLO into an error budget actually give a team?
options: A legal document protecting the company from customer lawsuits
A precise number engineering can spend against, deciding day to day how much deploy risk is acceptable
A way to avoid ever having to measure real user impact
A guarantee that no incident will ever occur during the period
mcqs.explanation: The error budget turns an abstract percentage into an operational number — a spendable allowance that governs deploy risk and pace day to day. It isn't a legal shield, doesn't remove the need to measure impact, and doesn't guarantee zero incidents — it defines how much unreliability is tolerable before something changes.

mcqs.question: A checkout service at 99.5% is asked to jump straight to 99.99%. What's the right first move?
options: Refuse the request outright since 99.99% is never realistic for checkout services
Agree immediately, since a stricter SLO is always better for the business
Name the architecture that number requires (e.g., multi-region active-active, synchronous replication) and its cost, then let actual revenue impact decide
Silently plan to hit 99.9% instead and report it as 99.99%
mcqs.explanation: The right move prices the number rather than reflexively accepting or rejecting it — naming the required architecture and its cost lets the business weigh that cost against real revenue at stake. Refusing outright skips the negotiation; agreeing blindly risks a commitment the architecture can't support; misreporting the actual number is dishonest and eventually catches up with you.

mcqs.question: Why is going from 99.9% to 99.99% reliability typically far more expensive than going from 99% to 99.9%?
options: Cloud providers charge a flat penalty fee for higher-nines contracts
Reliability gains are linear, so the cost is always proportional to the improvement
Each additional nine requires disproportionately more architecture (e.g., multi-region, synchronous replication), so cost rises non-linearly
99.99% is only achievable by switching to a completely different programming language
mcqs.explanation: The cost curve for reliability is non-linear — closing the last, smallest gaps in downtime typically demands categorically different architecture (cross-region synchronous replication, active-active topologies) rather than a proportional scale-up of the same approach. There's no such provider penalty fee, and language choice is irrelevant here.

mcqs.question: Why is committing to a 99.99% SLO on a single-region, asynchronously-replicated architecture a mistake?
options: The architecture cannot structurally deliver that reliability, so the commitment guarantees a future breach
99.99% is an illegal SLO target in most jurisdictions
Single-region architectures are always cheaper, so the mistake is purely financial
It's fine as long as the on-call team is large enough
mcqs.explanation: An SLO has to match what the architecture can actually deliver — a single-region, async-replicated setup has failure modes (a regional outage, replication lag) that make 99.99% structurally unreachable, no matter how well it's operated. This isn't a legal issue, purely a cost issue, or something a bigger on-call rotation fixes.
